🎙 UN Charter under fire: Why US attacks on Iran violate int'l law

📌 Tehran, IRNA – If states were free to attack one another based on their own assessments of possible future threats, what would be left of the international legal order? This question goes well beyond the political dispute between Iran and the United States.

It concerns one of the fundamental principles on which the international order established after the Second World War rests: the use of force is governed by law, and no state, however powerful, is entitled to place its own judgment above binding rules of international law.
​
The military attacks launched by the United States and the Zionist regime against Iran constitute a clear violation of the prohibition on the use of force and an infringement of Iran's sovereignty. Their legality must be assessed against the U.N. Charter and established principles of international law, not against political arguments or justifications advanced after military operations have begun.
​
Article 2(4) of the U.N. Charter prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. This prohibition is not merely a treaty obligation. It is also a fundamental rule of customary international law, as the International Court of Justice confirmed in its 1986 judgment in the Nicaragua case.
​
International law permits the use of force only in narrowly defined circumstances, including the exercise of the right of self-defense under Article 51 of the Charter. The U.S. military attack on Iran had no authorization from the Security Council, nor can allegations of possible future threats, in themselves, provide a sufficient legal basis for invoking self-defense. Article 51 recognizes the right of self-defense in the event of an armed attack. To treat a potential future threat as grounds for military action would be to accept preventive war based on the unilateral judgment of individual states. Such an interpretation would seriously undermine, if not altogether empty, the prohibition on the use of force of its practical meaning.
​
The legality of the U.S. attack has also been challenged within the American legal community. In a statement issued on March 6, 2026, the president of the American Branch of the International Law Association described the attack on Iran as unlawful, stressing that speculative threats concerning what might happen in the future cannot justify the use of military force.
​
The attacks on schools, sports stadiums, civilian infrastructure, and Iranian nuclear facilities subject to International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards raise further questions under international law. Apart from the prohibition on the use of force, these attacks must also be examined in light of the rules of international humanitarian law. Parties to an armed conflict are required to distinguish between military targets and civilians, refrain from disproportionate attacks, and take all feasible precautions to minimize harm to civilians and civilian infrastructure.
​
U.N. General Assembly Resolution 3314, which sets out the Definition of Aggression, identifies acts such as attacks by one state's armed forces against the territory of another and the blockade of a state's ports or coasts as acts of aggression. In the absence of a valid legal justification for the use of force, the U.S. military attack on Iran constitutes an internationally wrongful act for which the United States bears responsibility.
